text:
Generating an AI response takes seconds.
Knowing whether that response deserves to be trusted takes real skill. 👀
As GenAI tools become easier to use, the competitive advantage is shifting from simply creating outputs to evaluating them effectively.
A strong GenAI professional should be able to ask:
✅ Is the response factually accurate?
✅ Is it grounded in the right context?
✅ Does it follow the required instructions?
✅ Is it relevant, safe, and free from harmful bias?
✅ Will it remain reliable across different users and edge cases?
✅ Can its quality be measured consistently?
A polished answer is not necessarily a correct answer, and a successful demo is not automatically a dependable AI system.
That is why skills such as evaluation frameworks, test-dataset creation, hallucination detection, human feedback, guardrails, observability, and business-context validation are becoming essential.
The future will not belong only to people who can make AI generate more. It will belong to those who can determine whether what it generates is actually useful, reliable, and ready for the real world.
At Tutort Academy, we believe learning GenAI should go beyond prompting, toward building, testing, and improving AI systems that people can trust.

Preparing for a Senior Generative AI Engineer Interview? Can You Answer These 7 Advanced Technical Questions?
1. LLM Architecture & Model Selection
Your company needs an LLM for enterprise customer support. How would you choose between a proprietary model, an open-source model, and a fine-tuned solution based on accuracy, latency, privacy, and cost?
2. RAG Architecture & Retrieval Quality
Your RAG system retrieves relevant documents but still generates inaccurate answers. How would you optimize chunking, embeddings, hybrid search, reranking, and context construction?
3. Fine-Tuning vs. Prompt Engineering
When would you choose prompt engineering, RAG, or fine-tuning to improve an LLM's performance? Explain the trade-offs in cost, training data, maintainability, and accuracy.
4. Hallucination & Evaluation
Your LLM application produces fabricated facts in 12% of responses. How would you identify the causes, build an evaluation framework, and reduce hallucinations without making the system unnecessarily restrictive?
5. LLM Inference & Cost Optimization
Your application processes 5 million tokens daily, but inference costs exceed the budget by 40%. How would you optimize model selection, quantization, caching, batching, and token usage while maintaining response quality?
6. AI Agents & Tool Reliability
An AI agent uses external APIs to complete multi-step business workflows but occasionally repeats actions or executes tools incorrectly. How would you design state management, tool validation, retries, and safeguards against duplicate operations?
7. Production Deployment & Monitoring
Your Generative AI application serves 10,000 users daily. How would you monitor response quality, latency, token costs, safety, and model drift while ensuring reliable production performance?

Answer:
1. Build a representative evaluation dataset covering real user questions and edge cases.
2. Measure retrieval metrics such as Recall@K and Precision@K.
3. Check whether generated answers are supported by retrieved documents.

5. Test hallucination, relevance, and citation accuracy.
6. Include difficult queries, no-answer cases, and multi-document questions.

8. Track metrics continuously across model, prompt, and retrieval changes.
The goal is to measure the complete RAG pipeline, not rely on one accuracy number.

I recently went through a hiring process for an AI Fresher role, and I wanted to share my experience. There were 5 rounds: Aptitude → GD → AI Interview + Coding → Technical Interview → HR. I cleared the aptitude round and then attended the GD.
I was in Batch 7, with 13 candidates, and the GD lasted around 45 minutes. The interviewer started by asking everyone to introduce themselves, but somehow she missed calling my name 😄. I immediately unmuted and asked if I could introduce myself. She was very calm and friendly and apologized a few times. I introduced myself, talked about my recent project and technical skills, and also mentioned that one thing I currently lack is practical industry experience.
Then came the topic: “Will GenAI reduce software jobs or make software developers more productive?” I have a good grip on this topic, so I was ready to share my thoughts confidently. One person spoke before me, and I agreed with his point and added a few new points on how GenAI increases productivity in software work... As the discussion continued, I noticed that many candidates were already working in companies and were sharing examples from their real projects, bugs, and industry problems. Everyone was capable, and most of the discussion was going in the same direction, with people agreeing with each other.
So I took a chance and said something different: "I see that We are all agreeing that GenAI increases productivity and reduces workload, but what about freshers? If AI does most of the small tasks, how will freshers get real experience and grow into senior engineers?" I expected this to open up more discussion, but no one actually continued on my point. That's a separate matter, though. I spoke a total of 4 times during the GD.
What I want to share through is: there were some really strong candidates in that group, people who are already working and understand real industry problems and bugs firsthand. I realized that is exactly what I lack right now — real work exposure.
Still, it was a great learning experience to hear how things actually work in the industry.
And in case anyone's wondering if I cleared this round... I got the regret email already saying, "lot of competition" 😄 But no complaints, just learning and moving forward!

text:
Asked for a Senior LLM Optimization Engineer role at NVIDIA
Interviewer: Your team wants to reduce LLM inference costs by 50%, but product quality cannot drop significantly.
Question: What techniques would you evaluate, and how would you decide which optimization provides the best cost-quality trade-off?
Answer:
1. Start by measuring cost per request, tokens per request, latency, and quality to establish a baseline.
2. Use model routing so simple requests go to smaller, cheaper models.
3. Apply prompt and context optimization to reduce unnecessary input tokens.
4. Use caching for repeated prompts and responses.
5. Evaluate quantization such as INT8 or INT4 to reduce GPU memory and inference cost.
6. Test continuous batching to increase GPU utilization and throughput.
7. Consider smaller or distilled models for suitable workloads.
8. Run controlled A/B tests and compare cost savings, accuracy, latency, and user satisfaction.

text:
Lately, I've been interviewing AI Engineer candidates with 1–2 years of experience.
One thing surprised me.
Almost everyone can talk about RAG.
Almost everyone has built AI agents.
Most have used LangChain, LangGraph, OpenAI, Claude, or Gemini.
But when the conversation moves beyond frameworks...
...that's where many interviews start to slow down.
I ask simple questions like:
"Why do embeddings work?"
"Why does chunk size affect retrieval?"
"Why does an attention mechanism matter?"
"What actually happens before an LLM generates the first token?"
The room usually goes quiet.
It made me realize something.
We're getting really good at building AI applications.
But we're slowly skipping the fundamentals that make those applications reliable.
AI tools can write code.
They can generate APIs.
They can even scaffold an entire project.
But they can't replace your understanding.
If retrieval quality drops...
If latency suddenly doubles...
If hallucinations increase...
If your AI agent gets stuck in a loop...
The solution isn't another framework.
It's understanding what's happening underneath.
Frameworks will change.
Models will change.
The fundamentals won't.
That's why, before every interview, I'd rather revise concepts like:
→ Transformers
→ Attention Mechanism
→ Embeddings
→ Tokenization
→ Vector Search
→ HTTP & APIs
→ System Design
→ Memory
→ Databases
→ Evaluation
→ Python fundamentals
These are the concepts that help you explain why something works, not just how to build it.
If you're preparing for AI Engineer interviews, don't spend all your time learning the next framework.
Spend some time strengthening the foundation that every framework is built on.

• How does RAG work?

Why did you use this technology?
and then to
How did you measure the result?

→ Tools
→ Resources
→ Prompts
3. Explain the flow
→ User request
→ Model decides what it needs
→ MCP client communicates with the server
→ Server executes the required tool/resource
→ Result goes back to the model
4. Talk about the engineering layer
→ Authentication
→ Permissions
→ Error handling
→ Logging
→ Timeouts
→ Security
5. Then discuss the trade-offs
→ When should something be a tool vs a resource?
→ What happens if the MCP server is unavailable?
→ How would you handle multiple servers?
→ How would you prevent an unsafe tool call?
That is where the interview moves from:
“I know what MCP is”
to
“I know how I would build and operate one.”
For MCP interviews, don't prepare only definitions.
Prepare the architecture, request flow, implementation decisions and failure cases.

headline: AI/ML Engineer | Agentic AI & Multi-Agent Systems | Enterprise AI Platforms | MLOps & AI Observability | Building Production-Grade Intelligent Systems
text:
A good prompt is not just an instruction.
For RAG and agentic apps, it is a set of testable control blocks.
1. 𝗥𝗔𝗚 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗺𝗽𝘁𝘀 𝗡𝗲𝗲𝗱 𝗚𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴
→ Answer only from retrieved context
→ Give the model permission to refuse
→ Treat retrieved documents as data, not instructions
→ Tag sources and require citations
→ Define what happens when sources conflict
Retrieval decides what the model can say.
The prompt decides what it does with it.
2. 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗺𝗽𝘁𝘀 𝗡𝗲𝗲𝗱 𝗕𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗮𝗿𝗶𝗲𝘀
An agent also needs:
→ Clear tool descriptions
→ Explicit stopping conditions
→ Tool failure handling
→ Structured output contracts
→ Human approval for irreversible actions
The prompt states the rule. Code should enforce it.
3. 𝗦𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝗕𝗲𝗮𝘁𝘀 𝗠𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗪𝗼𝗿𝗱𝘀
“Be careful.”
“Be accurate.”
“Don’t hallucinate.”
These are weak controls.
Examples, schemas, refusal paths, source tags, and explicit conditions are much easier to test.
4. 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗺𝗽𝘁𝘀 𝗡𝗲𝗲𝗱 𝗘𝘃𝗮𝗹𝘀
Change one thing.
Run the eval set.
Compare the score.
Repeat.
A prompt without an eval set is just a guess with formatting.
The key lesson:
Grounding → Refusal → Delimiters → Citations → Conflict Rules → Tool Rules → Stopping → Failure Handling → Output Contract → Safety → Evals
Anyone can write a prompt.
Engineers know which block is missing.

headline: AI Engineer | Artificial Intelligence, Generative AI
text:
Asked for a Senior GenAI Engineer role at OpenAI
Interviewer: Your model has strong factual knowledge, but its responses don't match the tone and behavior your product requires. Would you use supervised fine-tuning, preference optimization, or prompt engineering?
Question: How would you identify which approach is appropriate, and what data would you need?
Answer:
1. Start with prompt engineering if the behavior can be controlled through clear instructions and examples.
2. If the model repeatedly fails to follow the desired behavior, consider supervised fine-tuning (SFT).
3. Use high-quality examples showing the desired input, response, tone, and behavior.
4. Consider preference optimization when multiple responses are possible and you need the model to prefer one style or behavior.
5.Collect preference data containing better and worse responses for the same input.
6. Create a representative evaluation set covering normal and difficult user scenarios.
7. Compare approaches using behavior consistency, quality, safety, latency, and cost.
8. Start with the simplest approach and move to fine-tuning only when prompting cannot reliably achieve the required behavior.
9. The key is matching the technique to the type of behavior problem and the quality of available training data.

text:
Asked in a Bloomberg AI/ML Engineer interview 👇
⠀
Your AI assistant processes financial reports. One incorrect decimal point changes executive decisions. How do you verify numerical correctness in LLM-generated outputs?
⠀
Most people answer "ask the model to double-check." A model re-reading its own answer repeats its own error. Verify with something that isn't a language model.
⠀
1. Extract numbers as structured data
- Pull values with units, period and source cell
- Never let the model do arithmetic in prose
⠀
2. Compute with code
- Totals, growth and ratios run in a calculator or SQL tool
- The LLM only narrates the result
⠀
3. Match every figure to its source
- Each number in the output must appear in the cited passage
- Flag anything that doesn't
⠀
4. Add sanity checks
- Sums reconcile, units agree, magnitude is plausible
⠀
5. Escalate on doubt
- Low-confidence figures go to a human with the source highlighted
⠀
The principle: numbers must be computed and checked, never generated.

text:
🧵 AI from Scratch · Post #11
Fine-Tuning — what it is and the 3 techniques that matter.
I hit a wall early in one of my projects. Perfectly capable LLM. But every time I gave it a specific task — map this JSON, stay in this format, respond only this way — it drifted.
Added things I didnt ask for. Behaved like a generalist when I needed a specialist. Prompt engineering helped.
RAG helped.
Neither fixed the core problem. The models behaviour needed to change. Thats when fine-tuning became the answer.
What it actually is.
Fine-tuning continues training a pre-trained model — but on a small, highly specific dataset. Your domain. Your tone. Your task. The weights shift. The model narrows. It stops being a generalist. 3 techniques that matter: Full Fine-Tuning Every weight updated. Maximum control. But needs huge data, expensive compute, and risks catastrophic forgetting — overwriting knowledge the model already had. LoRA Freeze the base model. Inject tiny trainable adapter layers alongside frozen weights.
Only adapters train — roughly 1% of a full fine-tunes cost.
I used this in JTAdmin — fine-tuned LLaMA on ~2,000 examples for a JSON mapping task. One overnight run on a single GPU. Worked consistently in production. Default choice for most builders.
RLHF Doesnt change what the model knows — changes how it behaves. Human raters rank outputs, a reward model learns their preferences, the LLM gets nudged toward better responses repeatedly.
This is what gives ChatGPT and Claude their judgment — when to push back, when to refuse, when to say I dont know.
When to use which:
→ Domain/tone/style → LoRA → Full behavioural overhaul → Full fine-tuning → Values and alignment → RLHF
